title: Why Your Rewards Points Are Making You Poorer
sources: American Airlines Group Inc., Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025 (SEC, filed Feb 2026): 'Cash payments from co-branded credit card and other partners were $6.2 billion and $6.1 billion during 2025 and 2024, respectively.' NOTE (hook wording): the $6.2B is cash from co-branded card AND other partners (mileage credits sold plus marketing services), so the script says 'from the banks and partners buying its points', not 'from selling points on cards' alone. Starting in 2026 Citi became the exclusive issuer of the AAdvantage co-branded card portfolio in the U.S. https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/6201/000000620126000014/aal-20251231.htm

American Airlines press release, fourth-quarter and full-year 2025 results (Jan 2026): full-year GAAP net income of $111 million on record revenue of $54.6 billion. Math: $6.2B / $0.111B = about 56x -> 'over fifty times what it kept in profit all year'. https://news.aa.com/news/news-details/2026/American-Airlines-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-financial-results-CORP-FI-01/default.aspx

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, Working Paper 2010-19, Agarwal, Chakravorti and Lunn, 'Why Do Banks Reward Their Customers to Use Their Credit Cards?' (rev. Dec 2010): a 1% cash-back reward raised spending by $68 a month and card debt by $115 a month during the first quarter of the program (an earlier version of the abstract reports $79 and $191). Math: 1% of $68 = $0.68. https://www.chicagofed.org/publications/working-papers/2010/wp-19

Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 'Credit Card Rewards: Issue Spotlight' (May 2024): over 1,200 rewards complaints in 2023 (+70% vs pre-pandemic); in one study rewards were on the front page of card offers over 94% of the time (APRs 28%); cardholders who revolve pay 94% of total interest and fees but gain less than 30% of rewards; a point is 'typically estimated by major issuers to be worth about $0.01'; issuers 'forfeit, expire, revoke, or otherwise take away hundreds of millions of dollars in earned rewards value each year'; themes include devaluation of earned rewards. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/issue-spotlight-credit-card-rewards/

S&H Green Stamps: Sperry & Hutchinson founded 1896; retailers bought the stamps from S&H and gave them to shoppers, who pasted them in books and redeemed them for catalog goods; in the 1960s the company issued more stamps than the U.S. Postal Service (Reader's Digest, June 1963, via Wikipedia 'S&H Green Stamps'). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S%26H_Green_Stamps
American Airlines AAdvantage launched May 1, 1981 (American Airlines corporate history), the first modern airline frequent-flyer program.

American Airlines Group Form 8-K (June 2020) and April-June 2020 investor disclosures: a third-party appraisal valued the AAdvantage program at $19.5 billion to $31.5 billion; the program was pledged as collateral for the CARES Act Treasury loan. American's stock-market value at the time was roughly $5.5-7 billion (View from the Wing, Apr/Jun 2020 coverage of the filings).

Delta SkyMiles, September 2023: changes announced Sept 13-14, 2023 caused a customer backlash; on Sept 25-27, 2023 CEO Ed Bastian said Delta 'probably went too far' and moved 'too fast'; Delta scaled back the changes on Oct 18, 2023 (AP, Fortune, Sept-Oct 2023).

U.S. Department of Transportation press release, Sept 5, 2024: USDOT opened an inquiry into the rewards programs of the four largest U.S. airlines (American, Delta, Southwest, United), covering devaluation of earned rewards, hidden or dynamic pricing, extra fees and reduced competition. https://www.transportation.gov/briefing-room/usdot-seeks-protect-consumers-airline-rewards-probe-four-largest-us-airlines-rewards

Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Public Policy Discussion Paper 10-3, Schuh, Shy and Stavins, 'Who Gains and Who Loses from Credit Card Payments? Theory and Calibrations' (2010): 'each cash-using household pays $149 to card-using households and each card-using household receives $1,133 from cash users every year.' https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/public-policy-discussion-paper/2010/who-gains-and-who-loses-from-credit-card-payments-theory-and-calibrations.aspx

Federal Reserve Board, FEDS working paper, Agarwal, Presbitero, Silva and Wix, 'Who Pays For Your Rewards? Redistribution in the Credit Card Market' (Jan 2023): about $15 billion a year is redistributed; regardless of income, sophisticated cardholders gain from reward cards at the expense of naive ones. https://www.federalreserve.gov/econres/feds/who-pays-for-your-rewards-redistribution-in-the-credit-card-market.htm

Federal Reserve G.19 Consumer Credit (via FRED series TERMCBCCINTNS): commercial bank credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest = 22.36% in August 2026. https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/TERMCBCCINTNS

Dave's numbers are an illustration (fictional but typical): 60,000-point bonus after $4,000 of spending in 3 months; normal card spending $900 a month ($2,700) -> $1,300 extra; 64,000 points x about 1 cent = about $640; $95 annual fee; about $90 of interest on the $1,300 carried for a few months at about 22% APR; total $1,300 + $95 + $90 = $1,485. Swipe fee 'about two percent' as in our credit card video (ep02).

alt_titles: Your "Free" Flight Cost You $1,485. Here's the Math.
Why Your Credit Card Points Cost More Than They Pay
youtube.hook: Banks and partners paid American Airlines about $6 billion in 2025, mostly for points on cards like yours. Who really pays for them, and how Dave kept $1,485 a year.
tags: are credit card points worth it
who pays for credit card rewards

Me hearing the words free flight.
There's just one tiny line at the bottom. You have to spend four thousand dollars on the card in your first three months.

Me deciding if I need a kayak.

Every shopping trip with a rewards card.

Same customers. Same cards. One tiny new reward. So what do you think happened to their spending?
It jumped by about seventy dollars a month. And the debt on those cards grew even faster.
Now look at that trade. One percent back on seventy dollars is seventy cents.

Me after earning seventy cents for spending seventy dollars.
So points don't pay you to shop. They get you to shop more and then they hand you back the crumbs.

Green stamps. Back in her day every time you bought groceries the shop gave you a strip of stamps. You licked them and stuck them in a book. And full books got you a toaster.

And here's the clever bit. The shop had to buy those stamps. And a shop only gets its money from one place. You.

Grandma realizing the toaster wasn't free.

While you think about it where do points even come from? The airline just makes them up on a computer. For free.

Which means the airline gets paid when I buy groceries. And when I fill my tank. And when I buy a kayak.
American Airlines' own yearly report says card companies and partners paid it about six billion dollars in cash last year.

So I'm not really the passenger. I'm the product.
Airlines in twenty twenty six.

Now back to your guess. According to the consumer bureau the big card companies themselves value a typical point at about one cent.
So my sixty four thousand points are worth about six hundred forty dollars. That's half of what I overspent to get them.
Me doing the points math.

It's like saving arcade tickets for the giant teddy bear and every time you get close the guy behind the counter quietly swaps the sign.
The rewards program when I finally have enough points.
And this happens to real people. In twenty twenty three Delta changed its SkyMiles rules so hard that customers revolted online.
Two weeks later the boss admitted they probably went too far. And Delta softened some of the changes.

So my flight is now twenty thousand points away. And the only way to get more points is to spend more.
Me staring at a second kayak.
But somebody else has been quietly paying for my points. Remember Grandma? She pays cash for everything.
I'm right in front of her at the checkout tapping my card. And every tap costs the shop about two percent of my bill.

It's B. And it's not close. People who carry a balance pay almost all of the interest and fees. And they take home less than a third of the rewards.
And after the kayak and the fryer and the big dinner I couldn't pay it all off. So the card started charging me around twenty two percent a year.
My points pay about one percent. That's like a shop that gives you a penny for walking in and charges you a quarter to leave.

card.t: I got played by a kayak.

beats.text: But here's what the smiley man at the booth doesn't want you to notice. This game only works on people who chase. And I just stopped chasing.
This part is education and not advice. I write three questions on a sticky note and wrap it around my card.
Question one. Would I buy this if there were no points? If the answer is no the points aren't a discount. They're the bait.
I try it and the extra shopping just stops. That keeps about thirteen hundred dollars a year at home.
Me walking past the kayak aisle now.
Question two. Can I pay the whole bill every single month? Because no reward on Earth keeps up with twenty two percent interest. So I turn on autopay for the full balance.
Question three. What does this card cost me just for existing? Mine was ninety five dollars a year. So I swap it for a boring one with no fee that just pays cash back.
And one rule for the points you already have. Spend them. Points aren't a savings account. They're milk. And there's a date on the carton you can't see.
My points sitting in the account for three years.
So I stop waiting for the eighty thousand point flight. I search a rainy Tuesday in the off season. Same beach. Fifty five thousand.
I book it on the spot. And then I turn around and look at the kayak.
So here I am. Same beach from the start of this video. On a flight my points really did pay for.
I can't get last year's money back. But this year it's staying in my pocket. And that's the whole trick.
Because points were never free money. They're a bill. And somebody always pays it. The shopper who buys more. The neighbor who pays cash. Or the person paying interest.
Your only job is to not be any of those three. Pay in full and never chase and spend your points fast. Then rewards can be a nice little extra.

slam.t: DON'T BE THE ONE WHO PAYS

beats.text: Oh and the kayak? I brought it with me. Turns out it floats.
So one point is worth about a penny. And the flight was never free. Somebody was always paying for it.
Whoever prints the points decides what they're worth. So don't let them decide what you buy.
Next time I find out why nobody at school ever taught me any of this. Not one class. Not one day.
Subscribe. It's free. And unlike your points it'll still be worth the same next year.
